title: Identification of the tensile damage of degraded carbon steel and ferritic alloy-steel by acoustic emission with in situ microscopic investigations
abstract: The paper presents results obtained from the destructive laboratory investigation conducted on materials from pressure vessels after long-term operation in the refinery industry. Tested materials contained structural defects, which arose from improper heat treatment during steel plate manufacturing. Detailed metallographic and chemical composition tests and static tensile tests were conducted. Next, complex tensile tests were conducted with simultaneous acoustic emission (AE) monitoring while observing microstructural changes by light microscopy. From the laboratory tests, the correlations between the AE signal parameters and material microstructural damage during the tensile tests were developed. The results will be used as a basis of new algorithms for the structural condition assessment of in-service pressure equipment.
journal: Archives of Civil and Mechanical Engineering

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The carbon and ferritic alloy steels with different chemical composition are widely used in various industrial branches, especially in pressure equipment used in the petrochemical and refinery industries. The pressure equipment, such as process piping, pressure vessels, reactors, boilers and columns, generally work under extreme conditions. Most of the pressure equipment has been operated for a few decades. The various types of hidden technological defects are present in such materials as a result of imperfections of the contemporary steel manufacturing technologies. Long-term operation of the pressure equipment under extreme conditions causes defect growth, crack propagation and damages in microstructure of the materials. The defects, which grew due to working loads, may damage the entire structures and, consequently, may also lead to the failure of the whole industrial unit. For example, the main reason of the failure of pipelines operated in the refinery and gas industries is material degradation (approx. 30%)  [1] .

Consequently, the development of new structural diagnostic methods, which allows the evaluation of the conditions of pressure equipment materials after long-term operation in the petrochemical and refinery industries, is very important. One of the modern and non-destructive evaluation (NDE) methods is the acoustic emission (AE) – the highly-sensitive, multi-parameter, passive,  in situ  NDE technique. The AE method is widely used in NDE health monitoring of various kinds of structures  [2]  in the field of petroleum, aerospace, automotive and construction. The advantages of the method are real time material degradation monitoring and high sensitivity to material failure. The AE method is also indispensable for the investigation of the kinetics of deformation and damage processes due to the capability to monitor local plastic deformation processes in the material.

The AE monitoring of in-service structural material condition is possible with the use of the AE criteria, which determine the type and stage of development of material's degradation/damage based on the AE signal parameters. Development of the AE criteria is possible as a result of complex destructive laboratory tests combining different experimental techniques. The criteria have to be regularly verified during the diagnostic tests of the in-service industry equipment.

The first attempts to laboratory study of AE generated during the plastic deformation and fracture of unnotched/notched specimens were conducted in the middle of the XXth century  [2] . One of the first correlations between the failure mechanisms (stress intensity factor) of different structural steels and the characteristic parameters of its AE signals were validated by Dunegan  [3] . For example, the total AE counts  N  and stress intensity factor  K  were correlated as  N

The AE behaviour in structural materials during deformation, fracture and other processes is still systematically examined with advances in the AE measuring systems and signal processing methods. Extensive studies of AE behaviour during tension of Armco (pure) iron and ultra-low carbon steels  [5–7]  as well as two-phased (ferrite-pearlite) low carbon steels (<0.2%C)  [8–17]  unnotched specimens were conducted. In case of plastic deformation of Armco iron specimens, AE is generated starting at the yield drop, followed by Lüders-band propagation and macroscopic strain localization associated with necking followed by crack nucleation and propagation.

As the result of the tensile process of structural low carbon steel (i.e. Q235, Q345 steels), the AE signals with characteristic features at different stages of loading are generated  [8–17] . Generally, the activity of AE increases near the yield point, but then the activity decreases significantly (exponentially  [9] ) when the material reaches the initial fracture region  [8,10,11,14] . At the early stage of plastic deformation (microyield stage), AE is generated by dislocation activity at grain boundaries, then a rapid increase of AE activity is observed after massive plastic deformation at yield  [11] . According to  [8,16] , the first low energy AE signals can be attributed to the dislocation multiplication and unpinning from Cottrell atmosphere or dislocation tangling. The latter AE signals may be generated by the simultaneous motion of high-density dislocations during Lüders-band propagation.

The AE method is also extensively used to study deformation and fracture processes, which occur in stainless steels with various chromium and nickel content. These are characterized by austenitic  [18–23] , austenitic–martensitic  [24]  and martensitic  [25–29]  microstructure. The influence of the carbide inclusion content in thermally aged AISI 316  [19,22,23]  and 304 grade  [18,20,21]  austenitic stainless steels on AE during tensile deformation was investigated. Significant changes were observed during AE generation by deformation process of sensitized stainless steel in comparison to solution annealed material. The sum of AE events of the thermally aged material is definitely lower than in annealed ones. This effect is caused by reduced dislocation mobility by diffusion of chromium or other elements and reduced dislocation activity due to the grain boundary strengthening. The deformation process of the aged austenitic stainless steel generates increased AE activity as a result of increased grain boundary cracking due to favourable size and morphology of carbide precipitates. In case of tensile deformation of cold-worked or pre-strained austenitic stainless steels the AE activity is definitely reduced as compared to solution annealed materials. The effect is as a result of reduced glide distance for moving dislocations and reduced rate of formation of dislocation avalanches  [20] .

The AE behaviour is different on several stages of the tensile process of quench and tempered steels (35CrMnSiA and 42CrMo steels with a different heat-treatments)  [25] . The AE parameters increase with the peak of rates around the yield point in uniform plastic deformation region. After that, in region of non-uniform plastic deformation, the AE event rates decrease  [26–29] . During plastic deformation of 35CrMnSiA steel AE signals with high amplitude and high energy are generated. This phenomenon does not occur in the steel without retained austenite. Moreover, the higher the content of retained austenite in the steel, the higher the number of AE events  [26] .

As the review of existing literature, the AE method is highly sensitive to the steels’ deformation and fracture during tensile testing. The AE method allows to attribute different AE signals for various deformation and damage mechanisms, like: dislocation glide, twinning, crack initiation and propagation in the structure materials. It is also worth noting that there are not many publications dedicated to this topic. Only a few works validated AE method by SEM observation of microstructural damage of aluminium alloys  [30–32]  and magnesium  [33] . It allowed them for a detail identification of the AE-sources.

This research was conducted in order to study the influence of microstructural degradation of carbon steel (0.2%C) and ferritic alloy steel (0.2%C–5.0%Cr–0.5%Mo, often called 5Cr–0.5Mo steel) on the AE, generated by the plastic deformation and fracture processes during quasi-static axial tension. The materials were cut out from pressure vessel shells, operated for many years in the refinery industry. The tensile tests of specimens with AE signals monitoring and  in situ  microstructural observations (during the test) by light microscopy were conducted. The results, obtained during the studies, will be used to develop AE criteria for the material condition assessment of in-service pressure vessels. It also will be used to make decisions about remaining life of such equipment with material degradation. The investigations presented in this paper were supported as a part of the project of LIDER VII Programme financed by the National Centre for Research and Development of Poland.

sections.heading: Materials
paragraphs: The specimens of two grades of structural steels, St3S/S235 and A335 P5 (designated as “St3S-used” and “A335-used”), were tested in this study. The materials are widely used in oil industry equipment. The first material – St3S hot-rolled low-carbon steel plate (wall thickness 16 mm) was obtained from crude oil distillation column shell operated for 50 years in a petroleum refinery. The distillation column shell plates were prepared in Ukraine according to the standard GOST 380–60  [34] . The second material – A335 P5 grade ferritic alloy steel seamless pipe (ø163 mm, wall thickness 7 mm) was obtained from furnace coil pipe of the crude oil distillation unit, operated for 6 years. The new materials with identical chemical composition as the used materials, such as S235 grade steel plate and A335 P5 tube with diameter 163 mm (designated as “S235-new” and “A335-new”) were also tested to conduct the comparative analysis.

The materials data and chemical composition are presented in  Tables 1 and 2 
                         
                         . The mechanical properties of tested steels are given in  Table 3 
                         . Tensile tests were conducted on the Zwick/Roell Z100 universal testing machine. The standard specimens were cut out in the axial direction of pipes and column.

Metallographic tests  used SEM and OM. The tested metallographic sections were machined from operated and the “new” materials in both circumferential and axial directions. The metallographic sections were cross-sectioned, mounted, polished and etched with the use of standard metallographic techniques.

Microscopic observations by OM of metallographic section of St3S steel showed overheated coarse-grained ferrite-pearlite microstructure ( Fig. 1 a and b)  with sharp shaped pearlite grains. Changes in the microstructure of the steel probably were as result of the lack of normalization treatment after hot rolling during the production period of steel plates. Steel with such a microstructure has tendencies for brittle fracture, reduced impact strength and mechanical properties such as  R

The microstructure of the furnace coil pipe material (material “A335-used”,  Fig. 2 a and b)  is significantly different from the microstructure of the unused pipe material (A335-new,  Fig. 2 c and d). The microstructure of first one is characterized by considerable heterogeneity and by numerous areas with directed grain growth (overheating structure features) and zones with patchy distribution of carbide precipitates, as well as depleted areas in carbides ( Fig. 2 a and b). The degradation changes in the morphology of the A335 P5 steel pipe's microstructure (A335-used), arose mainly as a result of its long-term overheating of material in a high temperature range (>600 °C). The SEM investigations showed that material of unused pipe (“A335-new”) is of its typical normalized steel microstructure with a ferritic matrix, mixed with precipitated carbides of chromium, molybdenum and iron ( Fig. 2 c and d).

sections.heading: Equipment and testing procedure
paragraphs: The specimens were axially loaded on the Zwick/Roell Z100 testing machine with hydraulic serrated grips. The use of hydraulic grips definitely reduces the noise level, generated in the sample mounting zone during the tensile test ( Fig. 3 a) . The static tensile tests with AE recording were conducted on unnotched flat specimens with gauge cross-section of 4 × 12 mm ( Fig. 3 b), machined from each material (St3S-used, S235-new, A335-used and A335-new). The specimens were cut out in the axial direction of pipes/column. The work zones of specimens (flat side of specimens between shoulders) were polished and etched with the use of portable metallographic techniques. The tests were conducted on four samples of each material. The AE signals were recorded by AMSY-6 digital multi-channel AE measurement system (ASIP-2 A channel type), which consists of: resonance sensors VS150-M and VS75-V type (resonance frequency of 150 kHz and 75 kHz); AEP4 external preamplifiers (amplification of 34 dB) – Vallen Systeme Company equipment.

As shown in  Fig. 3 a, AE was recorded by four sensors directly from the deformation zone. The force and displacement were recorded by the AMSY-6 system's parametric channels, which were connected to the output of the testing machine. The calibration of measurement channels was conducted with the use of the 2H/0.5 mm Hsu-Nielsen source according to the PN-EN 13554:2011 standard  [37] .

The monocular light portable microscope (magnification 200×, 400×, 600×) with digital camera was used for observation of the microstructural changes during the tensile tests. The microscope was mounted on a grip of the testing machine ( Fig. 3 a).

sections.heading: Results and discussion
paragraphs:
The representative tensile test results of a stress–displacement curves with AE signal parameter distribution and material microstructure images for each stage of tension are shown in  Figs. 4–8 
                      
                      
                      
                      
                      . Only AE signals located in the gauge zones of specimens were taken into account ( Figs. 4c, d and 5c, d ). The results of analysis demonstrated significant differences in parameters of AE signals (activity of AE, peak amplitudes, number of signals and energy), generated during the tensile testing of all types of materials.

The rapid increase of AE activity with the burst signal peak amplitudes approx. 45–50 dB ( Figs. 4a, b and 5a, b ) was recorded by all AE channels (CH1 to CH4) during tensile tests of materials designated as “St3S-used” and “S235-new”. The highest activity of the  RA  value ( RA 
                      = the rise time/the maximum amplitude  [2,38] ) was also noted when the materials reached the yield point ( Fig. 8 a–d). The  RA  values for signals, recorded by channels with VS75-V sensor type, were much higher than those recorded by VS150-M type sensors. It is found that AE at the early stage of plastic deformation, preceded by a yield point, is generated by dislocation movement at grain boundaries. Then rapid increase of AE activity is observed after massive plastic deformation – intensive development of slip bands (shear deformation on multiple slip planes) in ferrite grains as well as during Lüders-band propagation in the lower yield point  [5,8,11,16] .

The processes of intensive slip band formation in ferrite grains inhibit the material deformation after yield point (dislocation blocking). It is the start of the strain hardening stage. In this stage the dislocations accumulate, interact with one another, and serve as obstacles for their motion. This leads to a change of deformation mechanism from strong dislocation motion to short range motion. The strain hardening process requires higher stress level than earlier slip bands. The linear plastic deformation zones are formed in ferrite grains of low carbon steel as a result of strain hardening processes. These linear zones are directed to the tensile direction at an angle approx. 45°. These zones can already be observed with the use of OM ( Figs. 4f, g and 5f, g ) during the tensile test. The decrease of AE activity is observed during strain hardening stage ( Figs. 4a, b and 5a, b ).

The next stage is micro-crack formation process in the linear plastic deformation zones of ferrite grains ( Fig. 5 h and i). These processes started after reaching the maximum load. Each micro-cracking process generates a single burst signal with peak amplitudes approx. 50–60 dB. The growth and linkage of micro-cracks as well as macro-cracks development occurs on the final fracture stage while load decreases are observed ( Figs. 4 and 5 ).

Generally, the AE behaviour during the deformation of specimens machined from A335 P5 alloy steel seamless pipes (operated and unused pipe), was similar to low-carbon steels specimens ( Figs. 6 and 7 ). The AE signals with maximum burst peak amplitudes of approx. 55–60 dB were recorded at the yield point and at the moment of the linear plastic deformation zones forming in aged ferrite grains ( Fig. 6 ) during testing of unused “A335-new” material. The AE activity decreases at the next loading stage, when most of the microstructure ferrite grains contain the linear plastic deformation zones. The plastic deformation of the overheated microstructure of the “A335-used” material generates slightly higher AE activity than those generated in unused material ( Fig. 7 ). In this case the AE signals with maximum burst peak amplitudes of approx. 80–90 dB were recorded. During testing of both materials, measurement channels with VS150-M and VS75-V type sensors recorded a similar AE with similar parameters. It is worth noting that the plastic deformation and fracture of ferritic-perlitic microstructures of the St3S and S235 grade steels generated definitely higher AE activity than the ferritic microstructure of A335 P5 grade ferritic alloy steel.

Detailed analysis of AE signals frequency with the use of wavelet transform, analysis of other signal parameters (including the MONPAC technology), will be the subject of further research. The analysis will aim to closely identify the AE sources.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs:
1. 
                            The AE method allowed to detect early stages of plastic deformation and damage processes in long-term operated St3S grade carbon steel and A335 P5 grade ferritic alloy steel during quasi-static axial tension testing. 
                         
                         
                            2. 
                            The AE generated by microstructural damage processes of the steel was correlated to  in situ  microstructural observation with optical microscopy. 
                         
                         
                            3. 
                            The tested St3S grade carbon steel of a distillation column shell (operated for 50 years) showed overheated microstructures. The steel microstructure was coarse-grained with sharp shaped pearlite grains. These changes in the microstructural morphology probably resulted from the lack of normalizing heat treatment after the hot rolling of plates. 
                         
                         
                            4. 
                            The tested A335 P5 grade ferritic alloy steel of the furnace coil pipe (operated for 6 years) was overheated as a result of long-term operation in a high temperature range (>600 °C). The steel microstructure is characterized by considerable heterogeneity and by numerous areas with directed grain growth and zones with patchy distribution of carbide precipitates. 
                         
                         
                            5. 
                            The maximum of AE activity around yield point on their stress–strain curves has been observed as the only common feature of the tested materials. It is found that AE at the early stage of plastic deformation, preceded by a yield point, is generated by dislocation movement – intensive development of slip bands in plastic ferrite grains as well as during Lüders-band propagation. 
                         
                         
                            6. 
                            The decrease of AE activity is observed during strain hardening stage when the dislocations accumulate and serve as obstacles for their motion of limited distances – strain hardening processes. The linear plastic deformation zones in ferrite grains were observed by OM as a result showing localized deformation markings. 
                         
                         
                            7. 
                            The micro-cracks formation process in the linear plastic deformation zones of ferrite grains, near and after the maximum load, generates single burst signals with peak amplitudes of approx. 50–60 dB. The growth and linkage of micro-cracks as well as macro-cracks formation are found on the final fracture stage.
